Kalivoa / Kalivoa Academy / Understand your statistics Understand your statistics How do you calculate betting ROI and distinguish it from win rate? Kalivoa editorial team · October 8, 2026 ROI measures profit or loss relative to the amount staked. For settled cash bets without refunds or cash outs, calculate ROI = net profit ÷ total stakes × 100. Win rate answers a different question: what proportion of those bets won? A winning percentage alone does not describe the financial result. Choose your scope before calculating Choose a period and apply the same filters to every figure: bankroll, bookmaker, sport or bet type. Start with settled singles, cash stakes and one currency. Exclude pending bets from this example because their result is not yet known. Refunds, free bets and cash outs need an explicit convention. Before comparing your calculation with a tool’s figure, check which bets count towards stakes and wins. Percentages built on different scopes are not directly comparable. Separate gross returns from net profit Gross returns are the amount paid back for a slip. If they include the stake, subtract that stake to find net profit. For a lost bet without a refund, returns are zero and net profit equals the negative stake. Add net profits within your scope, then divide by the stakes placed on those bets. A bankroll deposit is not betting profit, and a withdrawal is not a sporting loss. Including them would change what ROI means. A real example: two lost bets and €17.50 staked Screenshots supplied by Jeremy on September 25, 2026 show two singles dated September 18: a tennis bet with a €10 stake and a cycling bet with a €7.50 stake. Both are marked lost with zero returns. Kalivoa’s history shows −€10 and −€7.50 respectively. The calculation is reproducible: −17.50 ÷ 17.50 × 100 = −100% ROI. For the same sample, 0 ÷ 2 × 100 = 0% win rate. This example covers only these two slips, not the complete bankroll or a month’s performance. Other slips are excluded from this scope. A real example: two lost bets and €17.50 staked Observed figure Tennis Cycling Example total Stake €10.00 €7.50 €17.50 Displayed returns €0.00 €0.00 €0.00 Net profit −€10.00 −€7.50 −€17.50 Winning bets 0 0 0 out of 2 Why do ROI and win rate tell different stories? Win rate counts outcomes. ROI also accounts for amounts staked and returned. Winning a small bet and losing a much larger one can produce a 50% win rate alongside a financial loss. Odds and stakes can also make two histories with the same win rate financially different. When comparing periods, review ROI, total stakes, settled bet count and win rate together. Check whether stake sizes changed. One percentage hides those differences. Past ROI does not predict the next result Two bets illustrate a calculation, not a conclusion about a betting method. A longer history still records past outcomes. ROI alone does not measure intermediate declines, financial exposure or the evidence attached to slips. Keep verifiable records of stakes and results, and do not increase stakes to recover a loss. Tracking helps you understand what was risked and lost; it guarantees no profit. Source: original slips and Kalivoa history supplied by Jeremy on September 25, 2026. This calculation covers only two lost singles dated September 18. Kalivoa / Kalivoa Academy / Understand your statistics Understand your statistics How do you read a bankroll’s drawdown in units? Kalivoa editorial team · October 8, 2026 Drawdown measures the decline from a curve’s previous high to a later point. For cumulative profit in units: drawdown = previous peak − current cumulative profit. Maximum drawdown is the largest such decline within the observed period. A positive final result can therefore coexist with a substantial decline along the way. Which curve should you use? First identify what the curve represents: balance, capital or cumulative profit. A public Kalivoa bankroll chart shows cumulative profits and losses in units. It does not show the actual bookmaker account balance. Choose a period and consistent history. Missing bets, corrected results or a different unit convention change the path. Reproducing a calculation requires the same starting point, bets and order. How do you calculate the decline step by step? Read results chronologically. After each settled bet, add its profit or loss to the running total. Keep track of the highest cumulative value reached so far, including the starting point. At each point, subtract the current cumulative value from that previous peak. A new high has zero drawdown at that instant. Retain the greatest decline to obtain maximum drawdown for your chosen scope. A recovery reduces current drawdown; it does not erase the maximum decline already experienced. A new peak becomes the reference for subsequent points. A real example: a 3.50 u decline from September 12 to 16 On October 8, 2026, EGS Betting’s public history showed a winning bet on September 12 followed by three losing bets on September 13, 15 and 16. Displayed losses were 1.25 u, 1 u and 1.25 u. No other entry was visible between those dates in that history. For this excerpt, set the origin to 0 u immediately after the September 12 bet. This zero is a calculation reference, not the tipster’s capital. The losses then produce cumulative changes of −1.25 u, −2.25 u and −3.50 u. Maximum decline within this excerpt is 0 − (−3.50) = 3.50 u. It must not be presented as the complete bankroll’s maximum drawdown. A real example: a 3.50 u decline from September 12 to 16 Excerpt point Added outcome Cumulative change Decline from excerpt peak After the September 12, 2026 bet Reference point 0 u 0 u September 13, 2026 −1.25 u −1.25 u 1.25 u September 15, 2026 −1 u −2.25 u 2.25 u September 16, 2026 −1.25 u −3.50 u 3.50 u Why does the page show 4.15 u maximum drawdown? At the same observation, the page displayed 25 settled bets, +9.41 u cumulative profit and “Drawdown max” of −4.15 u. That figure covers the complete displayed series; our table covers only September 12–16. The negative sign describes a decline; its depth is 4.15 u. Final profit gives the final cumulative result. Drawdown describes the decline from an earlier peak. A positive result does not mean a path without losses. 4.15 u does not automatically mean 4.15% of capital Expressing a decline as a percentage of capital requires the peak capital and a compatible capital series: relative decline = (peak capital − capital after decline) ÷ peak capital × 100. Cumulative profit can start at zero or become negative. Dividing drawdown by that profit does not give a meaningful capital percentage. The tipster’s private cash amounts are unknown, so we do not convert this drawdown into euros or an account percentage. Which limits matter? Period, sampling frequency and bet order affect drawdown. Daily grouping can hide a peak or trough between bets. Check those conventions and bet count before comparing histories. Drawdown does not prove that every slip was verified or cap future losses. Read evidence, ROI and curve declines separately. Do not increase stakes to recover an earlier peak: tracking helps you understand exposure and personal limits. Source: EGS Betting’s public bankroll, observed on October 8, 2026 after reviewing 25 visible bets. Calculations use losses from September 13, 15 and 16. Values can change. Kalivoa / Kalivoa Academy / Read a tipster’s bet evidence Read a tipster’s bet evidence Why does a public bankroll display stakes in units? Kalivoa editorial team · October 8, 2026 A unit, written “u”, expresses a stake relative to a reference chosen by the bettor. It lets readers see stake sizes without directly publishing their euro amounts. One unit is not a universal cash amount: its conversion depends on the reference used. It proves neither the bookmaker account balance nor the reliability of a pick. Why display 1 u instead of a cash amount? Two people can stake different cash amounts while calling each stake one unit. The public figure provides a relative scale for reading the history. Without the conversion rule, you cannot reconstruct the author’s actual cash stakes. Units help compare stakes within one history. A 2 u stake is twice a 1 u stake when both entries use the same reference. This does not mean the second bet is twice as likely to win. How does conversion work? The conversion is: stake in units = cash stake ÷ cash value of one unit. You need both amounts and a consistent convention. Educational illustration, not a real slip: if one unit is €20, a €30 stake is 1.5 u. This explains a scale, not a recommended stake or an observation of EGS Betting’s bankroll. A tool can freeze units when a bet is recorded, then use a separate setting to show a reader’s private cash equivalent. The reader’s personal equivalent does not reveal the author’s actual stake. In Kalivoa, check the settings and proposed units before confirming an import. In Kalivoa, one unit corresponds to 1% of the bankroll’s reference amount. That amount is a conversion setting; it does not prove the balance available at the bookmaker. A real public bankroll example On October 8, 2026, EGS Betting’s public bankroll displayed 26 bets: 25 settled and one pending. Its certification panel showed 2.5 u of tracked volume and an “Under observation” status with a score of 10/100. These figures were recorded from the public page with the tipster’s consent. Total history count and certification volume cover different scopes. Imported history must be distinguished from the portion tracked since certification activation. Dividing 2.5 u by 26 would not establish the complete bankroll’s average stake. A real public bankroll example Observed public figure What it tells you 26 visible bets History entries at the time of observation 25 settled, 1 pending The status breakdown on that date 2.5 u certification tracked volume The tracked scope displayed by the panel, not all historical stakes Under observation The displayed status, not completed certification What should you check before comparing histories in units? Start with the period and included bets. Check whether the author explains the convention, stakes and results are visible, and reference changes affect interpretation. Do not compare certification volume with all stakes in another bankroll. Then review the evidence attached to slips. A history can be readable in units without complete evidence. Stake format explains how amounts are expressed; evidence status explains what lets you check a bet. Units do not remove financial risk Calling a loss “u” does not make it virtual. A stake still represents money exposed under the applicable conversion. Unit tracking guarantees no future profit and does not justify copying a tipster’s stakes. Set personal limits and use responsible gambling resources if needed. Source: EGS Betting’s public bankroll, observed on October 8, 2026 with consent. Kalivoa / Kalivoa Academy / Keep your betting history Keep your betting history How do you track an accumulator without counting its stake twice? Kalivoa editorial team · October 8, 2026 Record the accumulator once, with the slip’s stake and total odds. Attach every selection to that bet. Two selections within one accumulator are not two singles: entering the full stake against each would artificially double the amount staked in your records. What counts as one bet? An accumulator combines several selections under one shared stake. The main history entry holds that stake, the total odds and the overall result. Its selection details explain what you backed without adding another stake. If you also placed a single on one of those selections, that is a separate slip with its own stake. Keep one entry for the single and another for the accumulator. The number of entries follows actual slips, not the number of sporting picks. What should you check before saving? Start by counting the selections on the original slip. Compare each event, market and pick with the proposed details in Kalivoa. Correct missing selections or incorrectly read names before confirming. Enter the shared stake at bet level. Check each selection’s odds separately from the bookmaker’s displayed total odds. Use the displayed total for the slip: rounding, boosted odds or bookmaker rules can make a calculation from visible selection odds differ from that total. Screenshot imports still require review. Kalivoa does not request bookmaker account access: compare the proposed fields with your original slip. Which result should you record if one selection loses? Use the overall slip status settled by the bookmaker. Do not infer its financial result from one match alone: void selections, refunds, cash outs or special offers can affect settlement. Keep an unsettled slip pending. If its result is unreadable, check the source before selecting a status. Selection details document the bet; the history entry’s result applies to the complete slip. How do you spot a duplicate in your history? After saving, find the accumulator by date and event, then expand its selections. Make sure only one entry carries its stake. The same participants can appear on other legitimate slips: compare time, market and stake before deciding an entry is a duplicate. If several screenshots show different parts of one slip, compare the proposed bets before saving them. Complementary views should not turn into duplicate bets. Correct confirmed duplicates before interpreting your statistics. A real example: two selections and one €11.25 stake Screenshots supplied by Jeremy on September 25, 2026 show a tennis accumulator and its Kalivoa history entry. These observations illustrate accumulator structure. They do not measure OCR accuracy or provide a profit calculation example. Mistakes that distort your records Creating a single for every selection and repeating the accumulator’s full stake. Saving the same slip twice from overlapping screenshots. Replacing the settled total odds with a multiplication of rounded selection odds. Confusing a selection’s result with the final settlement of the slip. Kalivoa / Kalivoa Academy / Tipster transparency Tipster transparency How can you verify a tipster's published bets? Open the tipster's public bankroll, then review results, bet evidence and the time period separately. A profitable history alone does not show that every slip was verified. The transparency log shows the scans and corrections linked to an individual bet. Three checks to make 1 Check the period and number of bets See how many bets are visible, how many have settled and when they were recorded. A short run or a single result cannot establish future performance. 2 Read the evidence status of each bet Open the transparency log. “Evidence received”, “Limited evidence” and “Certified” mean different things. A slip scanned before the event and a result confirmed by a second scan provide the most complete evidence cycle. 3 Compare the history with the overall status An older bet may remain visible without counting towards certification, which starts when the bankroll is published. Read the displayed score and level, and the visible corrections, separately from profit and ROI. Real example: EGS Betting's public bankroll On October 8, 2026, we reviewed EGS Betting's public page with the tipster's permission to cite it. These are the values displayed at that point in time, not a performance promise or live figures. Observed October 8, 2026 Visible bets 26, including 25 settled and 1 pending Kalivoa certification 10/100 · Under observation Bets with complete evidence 0% Volume tracked for certification 2.5 units The pending bet dated October 8 displayed “Evidence received”; a settled bet dated October 4 displayed “Limited evidence”. These labels show why it is useful to inspect individual bets instead of describing the whole bankroll with one number. Open EGS Betting's public bankroll ↗ Why “Under observation” if 25 bets are settled? The visible total includes historical bets. Certification tracking begins when the bankroll is published and does not retroactively certify earlier bets. The currently deployed rule keeps the overall level “Under observation” until at least 10 settled bets are eligible since activation. The 25 visible results are therefore not 25 eligible proofs. What certification shows, and its limits Kalivoa rates the evidence attached to published bets; it does not verify the actual bookmaker account balance. The score cannot guarantee that cheating is impossible or that a tipster will profit in future. The tipster's real stake amounts remain private: the page displays stakes and results in units. Kalivoa / Kalivoa Academy / Bet slip review Bet slip review What should you check after scanning a betting slip? Before saving a bet read from a screenshot, compare every proposed field with the original slip. Check at least the selection, odds, stake and result. Also review the date, bet type, bankroll and free-bet status when relevant. Correct anything uncertain before confirming. Why review extracted details? A wrong stake or result affects profit and statistics. Incorrect odds change the calculation for a winning bet. A wrong selection makes the history harder to verify. Screenshot reading helps with entry, but it does not replace your review. Checklist before saving 1 Count the bets Compare the proposed bets with the slips visible in the image. For a multiple, review every selection. Avoid adding the same slip twice if it appears in more than one screenshot. 2 Compare the event and selection Check the sport, market, participants and actual pick. Two markets on the same event are not interchangeable. 3 Check odds and stake Read the numbers on the original slip, including decimal separators. Incorrect odds or stake make financial results harder to interpret. 4 Review date and status Fill in missing fields. For a settled slip, compare win, loss, refund or cash out with what the slip shows. Do not guess unreadable information. 5 Choose the right bankroll Assign the bet to the intended bankroll and review its free-bet status. A free stake is not the same as money actually risked. 6 Review once more, then save After confirming, open your history to ensure the bet appears once with the corrected details. A real review screen This screenshot supplied by Jeremy shows two single bets proposed for review in Kalivoa, one for tennis and one for cycling. Selections, odds, stakes and results are visible. The dates are still blank: they need checking before saving. Screenshot supplied on September 25, 2026. It shows the review step, not a measured speed or overall reading accuracy. No ticket reference or account identifier is visible. What if the slip was read incorrectly? Correct the proposed fields before saving. If a selection or result is uncertain, return to the original slip. If the image cannot settle the question, enter the bet manually instead of guessing. Kalivoa does not request bookmaker account access to import a screenshot. Kalivoa / Académie Kalivoa / Comprendre ses statistiques Comprendre ses statistiques Comment calculer le ROI de ses paris et le distinguer du taux de réussite ? Rédaction Kalivoa · 8 octobre 2026 Le ROI mesure le bénéfice ou la perte par rapport aux mises engagées. Pour un ensemble de paris réglés en argent réel, sans remboursement ni cash out, calculez ROI = bénéfice net ÷ total des mises × 100. Le taux de réussite répond à une autre question : quelle proportion de ces paris a été gagnée ? Un pourcentage de paris gagnés ne suffit donc pas à décrire le résultat financier. Définissez le périmètre avant de calculer Choisissez une période et gardez les mêmes filtres pour tous les chiffres : bankroll, bookmaker, sport ou type de pari. Pour commencer, sélectionnez des paris simples réglés, avec des mises en argent réel et une devise commune. Laissez les paris en attente hors de cet exemple : leur résultat n’est pas encore connu. Les remboursements, freebets et cash outs demandent une convention explicite. Avant de rapprocher votre calcul d’un chiffre affiché par un outil, vérifiez quels paris entrent dans le total des mises et dans le décompte des gagnants. Deux pourcentages construits sur des périmètres différents ne sont pas directement comparables. Distinguez retour brut et bénéfice net Le retour brut correspond à la somme reversée pour le ticket. Lorsqu’il inclut la mise, il faut retirer celle-ci pour obtenir le bénéfice net. Pour un pari perdu sans remboursement, le retour est nul et le bénéfice net est négatif : il vaut l’opposé de la mise. Additionnez ensuite les bénéfices nets des paris du périmètre. Ce total se rapporte aux mises engagées dans ces paris. Un dépôt dans la bankroll n’est pas un bénéfice de pari ; un retrait n’est pas une perte sportive. Les intégrer au numérateur changerait la signification du ROI. Exemple réel : deux paris perdus, 17,50 € engagés Les captures fournies par Jeremy le 25 septembre 2026 montrent deux paris simples datés du 18 septembre : un pari de tennis avec une mise de 10 € et un pari de cyclisme avec une mise de 7,50 €. Tous deux sont indiqués comme perdus, avec un retour nul. L’historique Kalivoa affiche respectivement −10 € et −7,50 €. Le calcul est reproductible : −17,50 ÷ 17,50 × 100 = −100 % de ROI. Pour ce même échantillon, 0 ÷ 2 × 100 = 0 % de réussite. Cet exemple porte uniquement sur ces deux tickets. Il ne décrit pas le résultat de la bankroll complète, ni un mois de performance. Les autres tickets sont exclus de ce périmètre. Rédaction Kalivoa · 8 octobre 2026 Le drawdown mesure la baisse entre le plus haut atteint par une courbe et un point qui le suit. Sur une courbe de bénéfice cumulé en unités : drawdown = sommet précédent − bénéfice cumulé actuel. Le drawdown maximal est la plus grande de ces baisses sur la période observée. Un résultat final positif peut donc coexister avec une baisse importante en cours de route. Quelle courbe faut-il observer ? Précisez ce que représente la courbe : un solde, un capital ou un bénéfice cumulé. La bankroll publique Kalivoa montre les bénéfices et les pertes cumulés en unités. Elle ne représente pas le solde réel du compte bookmaker. Choisissez une période et un historique cohérent. Des paris manquants, des résultats corrigés ou une autre convention d’unités changent le parcours. Pour reproduire un calcul, conservez le même point de départ, les mêmes paris et le même ordre. Comment calculer la baisse, étape par étape ? Parcourez les résultats dans l’ordre chronologique. Après chaque pari réglé, ajoutez son bénéfice ou sa perte au cumul. Gardez en mémoire le plus haut cumul déjà atteint, en incluant le point de départ. À chaque point, soustrayez le cumul actuel de ce sommet précédent. Un nouveau sommet a une baisse nulle à cet instant. Conservez la plus grande baisse rencontrée pour obtenir le drawdown maximal du périmètre. Une remontée réduit le drawdown courant ; elle n’efface pas la baisse maximale déjà traversée. Un nouveau sommet devient la référence pour les points suivants. Exemple réel : une baisse de 3,50 u du 12 au 16 septembre Le 8 octobre 2026, l’historique public d’EGS Betting montrait un pari gagné le 12 septembre, puis trois paris perdus les 13, 15 et 16 septembre. Les pertes affichées étaient de 1,25 u, 1 u et 1,25 u. Aucune autre ligne n’était visible entre ces dates dans cet historique. Pour lire cet extrait, plaçons l’origine à 0 u juste après le pari du 12 septembre. Ce zéro est un point de référence du calcul, pas le capital du tipster. Les pertes donnent ensuite −1,25 u, −2,25 u et −3,50 u de variation cumulée. La baisse maximale de cet extrait est donc 0 − (−3,50) = 3,50 u. Elle ne doit pas être présentée comme le drawdown maximal de toute la bankroll. Exemple réel : une baisse de 3,50 u du 12 au 16 septembre Point de l’extrait Résultat ajouté Variation cumulée Baisse depuis le sommet de l’extrait Après le pari du 12/09/2026 Point de référence 0 u 0 u 13/09/2026 −1,25 u −1,25 u 1,25 u 15/09/2026 −1 u −2,25 u 2,25 u 16/09/2026 −1,25 u −3,50 u 3,50 u Pourquoi la page indique-t-elle un drawdown maximal de 4,15 u ? Au même relevé, la page publique affichait 25 paris réglés, un bénéfice cumulé de +9,41 u et un « Drawdown max » de −4,15 u. Ce dernier chiffre concerne toute la série affichée ; notre tableau décrit seulement l’extrait du 12 au 16 septembre. Le signe négatif de l’interface décrit une baisse ; sa profondeur est de 4,15 u. Le bénéfice final donne le résultat cumulé à la fin. Le drawdown décrit le recul depuis un sommet antérieur. Un bilan positif ne signifie pas une progression sans pertes. 4,15 u ne signifie pas automatiquement 4,15 % du capital Pour exprimer une baisse en pourcentage de capital, il faut connaître le capital au sommet et utiliser une série de capital compatible : baisse relative = (capital au sommet − capital après la baisse) ÷ capital au sommet × 100. Le bénéfice cumulé peut commencer à zéro ou devenir négatif. Diviser la baisse par ce bénéfice ne donne pas un pourcentage de capital exploitable. Les montants privés du tipster ne sont pas connus : nous ne convertissons pas son drawdown en euros ou en pourcentage de son compte. Quelles limites garder en tête ? La période, la fréquence des points et l’ordre des paris influencent le drawdown. Un regroupement par jour peut masquer un sommet ou un creux entre deux paris. Vérifiez ces conventions et le nombre de paris avant de comparer des historiques. Le drawdown ne prouve pas que tous les tickets sont vérifiés et ne fixe pas un plafond aux pertes futures. Lisez séparément les preuves, le ROI et les baisses de la courbe. Ne relevez pas vos mises pour retrouver un ancien sommet : le suivi sert à comprendre votre exposition et vos limites. Kalivoa / Académie Kalivoa / Lire les preuves d’un tipster Lire les preuves d’un tipster Pourquoi une bankroll publique affiche-t-elle les mises en unités ? Rédaction Kalivoa · 8 octobre 2026 Une unité, notée « u », exprime une mise par rapport à une référence définie par le parieur. Elle permet de lire la taille des mises sans publier directement leur montant en euros. Une mise de 1 u n’est pas un montant universel : sa conversion dépend de la référence utilisée. Elle ne prouve ni le capital disponible sur un compte bookmaker ni la fiabilité d’un pronostic. Pourquoi afficher 1 u au lieu d’un montant en euros ? Deux personnes peuvent engager des montants différents tout en décrivant leur mise comme une unité. Le chiffre public donne alors une échelle relative pour lire l’historique. Sans connaître la règle de conversion, il ne permet pas de retrouver les montants réellement engagés par l’auteur. Pour le lecteur, les unités aident à comparer les mises d’un même historique. Une mise de 2 u représente deux fois une mise de 1 u lorsque les deux lignes utilisent la même référence. Cela ne signifie pas que le deuxième pari a deux fois plus de chances de gagner. Comment expliquer une conversion ? La conversion s’écrit : mise en unités = mise en devise ÷ valeur d’une unité dans cette devise. Il faut connaître les deux montants et appliquer la même convention. Illustration pédagogique, sans ticket réel associé : si la valeur d’une unité est fixée à 20 €, une mise de 30 € correspond à 1,5 u. Ce calcul explique le fonctionnement d’une échelle ; il n’est ni une recommandation de mise ni une observation de la bankroll d’EGS Betting. Un outil peut utiliser une référence pour figer les unités à l’enregistrement, puis une autre pour afficher un équivalent privé au lecteur. Ces deux opérations doivent être distinguées : l’équivalent personnel affiché à un visiteur ne révèle pas le montant réel du ticket de l’auteur. Dans Kalivoa, vérifiez les réglages et les unités proposés avant de valider un import. Dans Kalivoa, la valeur d’une unité correspond à 1 % du montant de référence défini pour la bankroll.
